links.outcome: Lay perceived empathy, reliability, comprehensibility and willingness to follow AI medical advice with vs without disclaimer
links.effect: Study 1: no significant effect on any outcome (all p > .17). Study 2: no effect on empathy, reliability, comprehensibility (all p > .19); willingness to follow slightly lower (p = .039), not significant after multiple-testing correction.
links.quote: In study 1, the disclaimer did not significantly affect any outcome (all p > .17).

links.outcome: Effect of disclaimer about AI error risk on laypeople's reliability ratings and willingness to follow advice
links.effect: Stronger disclaimer highlighting higher error risk than physicians did not significantly change reliability (all p > .19); willingness to follow slightly lower (p = .039) but not significant after correction; no difference between disclaimers.
links.quote: Willingness to follow the advice was slightly lower with the disclaimer (p = .039), but this effect did not remain significant after correcting for multiple testing.

links.outcome: Whether disclaimers on AI limitations change perception of and willingness to follow AI medical advice
links.effect: Disclaimers had no significant effect on empathy, reliability, comprehensibility; willingness to follow slightly lower in study 2 (p = .039) but not after multiple-testing correction.
links.quote: Disclaimers may thus serve mainly as transparency and liability measures and should not be relied on alone to protect users.

unlisted_practices: Communicating uncertainty within the AI response as an alternative to disclaimers (suggested, not tested)
